chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Makes a Stock Cyclical or Defensive

lessons.title: Cyclical vs Defensive: It's About Earnings, Not Share Price

body.text: A stock is cyclical or defensive because of what happens to its profits when the economy slows. Not because its share price is volatile, not because of its P/E, and not because of what it did in one bad month.

children.text: Most investors sort stocks into cyclical and defensive by gut feel. Steel feels risky, soap feels safe. That instinct is roughly right, but it breaks down the moment you need it most: when you are deciding what to hold going into a slowdown, or whether a stock that has just fallen 30% is a bargain or a warning. This lesson gives you the one test that actually separates the two, and the rest of the course builds on it.
The Only Test That Matters

markDefs.definition: A company whose revenue and especially profits rise sharply when the economy is expanding and fall sharply, sometimes into losses, when it contracts.
A company whose revenue and profits stay relatively stable through economic booms and slowdowns, because demand for what it sells does not depend much on the economy.

children.text: Ask one question: when GDP growth slows, consumers tighten budgets, and companies cut capex, what happens to this company's earnings? A
cyclical stock
sees profits fall hard, often far more than revenue. A
defensive stock
keeps earning roughly what it earned before, and often keeps growing, because people do not stop brushing their teeth or switching on the lights in a recession.

body.title: Cyclical vs Defensive at a Glance

columns.label: Cyclical
points: Sells things buyers can postpone: cars, homes, steel, machinery
Selling prices often set by global commodity markets, not the company
High fixed costs, so a small revenue drop hits profit hard
Profits can swing from record highs to losses within two or three years
Indian examples: Tata Steel, Hindalco, Maruti Suzuki, UltraTech Cement, L&T

columns.label: Defensive
points: Sells things people keep buying: soap, food, medicines, electricity
Strong brands or regulated pricing let it protect margins
Costs and volumes move gradually, so profits are predictable
Profits tend to grow steadily, with shallow dips at worst
Indian examples: Hindustan Unilever, Nestle India, Power Grid, Colgate-Palmolive India

children.text: Two Companies Through One Cycle
Take two illustrative companies with the same starting revenue of ₹10,000 crore. CycleCo makes steel. StapleCo makes soaps and detergents. Watch what five years of one economic cycle does to each.

stats.context: Profit grew every year of the cycle

children.text: Notice the gap between revenue and profit. CycleCo's revenue fell 32% from peak to trough, but its profit did not fall 32%. It disappeared entirely and turned into a loss. That amplification is the signature of a cyclical business, and Chapter 2 explains exactly where it comes from.

body.caption: Use this to compare how far revenue and profit moved in the same period

body.title: Measure the Swing
body.prompt: Using the table above, by what percentage did CycleCo's net profit fall from Year 2 (₹1,600 crore) to Year 3 (₹500 crore)? Enter the size of the fall as a positive number.
body.explanation: (500 - 1,600) / 1,600 × 100 = -68.75%. Over the same year, revenue fell only 16%, from ₹12,500 crore to ₹10,500 crore. A 16% revenue dip wiping out more than two thirds of profit is exactly what makes a stock cyclical.

children.text: Real Indian Companies, Same Pattern

The illustration is not exaggerated. Tata Steel posted a record consolidated net profit of over ₹40,000 crore in FY22, when global steel prices were near their highs. Two years later, in FY24, it reported a consolidated net loss as steel prices cooled and its European operations bled. Hindustan Unilever, over the same stretch and through the FY21 lockdown year, kept reporting growing profits. Same country, same economy, completely different earnings behaviour.

body.caption: Why these businesses behave the way they do

cells: Construction and auto demand falls, global steel prices drop
Buyers postpone purchases, higher loan rates hurt affordability
Housing and infrastructure construction slows, prices soften
People still buy daily essentials, maybe smaller packs
Earns regulated returns set by CERC, largely independent of demand swings

children.text: Why Share Price Is the Wrong Test
The tempting shortcut is to look at price charts: if a stock fell hard, it must be cyclical; if it held up, it must be defensive. This fails for three reasons.
Panics hit everything.

The Nifty 50 fell close to 40% between January and March 2020. Defensive names like HUL fell sharply too, even though their earnings barely wobbled. A single crash tells you about fear, not about the business.
Defensives can derate.

A consumer staples stock bought at 70 times earnings can fall 25% while its profit grows every quarter, simply because the market decides to pay 50 times instead. The price fell, the business stayed defensive.
Cyclicals can rally in a slowdown.

Markets look 6 to 12 months ahead, so metal and auto stocks often bottom and start rising while their reported profits are still falling. Price movement and earnings movement are frequently out of sync for cyclicals.

body.text: Never classify a stock from one year of data or one market fall. Pull up at least 8 to 10 years of annual profits, which ideally covers one full economic cycle, and look at how deep the dips were. That is the evidence. Everything else is a guess.

body.title: What Counts as Evidence?
body.question: Which of these is the strongest evidence that a company is defensive?
options: Its share price fell less than the Nifty 50 last month
Its net profit held steady or grew through past slowdowns, including FY21
It trades at a low P/E compared with the market
It pays a high dividend yield
body.explanation: Defensiveness is about earnings stability through bad economic periods. One month of price action reflects sentiment. A low P/E often shows up in cyclicals at peak earnings, which Chapter 4 covers. A high dividend yield can come from a falling share price or a one-time payout, not a stable business.

body.title: The Office WhatsApp Group Argument
body.scenario: A colleague posts in your office investing group: 'This packaged food stock is down 18% in a year while that auto stock has doubled. The food company is clearly the risky cyclical one, time to switch.' You check Screener.in. The food company's net profit grew about 9% a year for the last decade with no losses. The auto company's profit has tripled this year, but it made losses in two of the last eight years.
body.prompt: Is your colleague's classification right? What would you tell the group?
body.modelAnswer: No. The classification is backwards. The food company's earnings grew steadily for a decade, which makes it defensive, and its 18% fall is most likely a valuation derating or a temporary concern rather than a sign of cyclical earnings. The auto company has already swung from losses to strong profits, which is textbook cyclical behaviour, and a doubling price after profits tripled could mean it is closer to a peak than a start. Switching based on the last year of price moves means buying the cyclical after its earnings recovery is already visible. Neither stock is automatically a buy or sell, but the argument confuses price momentum with business stability.

children.text: Why This Matters for Your Money

Getting this label right changes almost every decision you make. It decides which valuation tool works: a low P/E on a cyclical at peak profits is a trap, while a high P/E on a defensive may be justified. It decides how much of a fall you should expect in the next downturn. And if you invest through mutual funds, it tells you what you really own: a flexi-cap fund heavy on metals, autos, and capital goods will behave very differently in a slowdown from one tilted towards FMCG and pharma, even if both carry the same risk label on the factsheet.

body.label: The one-line test
body.value: Check whether profits held up in the last slowdown
body.context: Look at FY20 and FY21 on Screener.in for any Indian listed company, then go back further to FY09 if the history is available

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Search any NSE or BSE listed company and scroll to the Profit and Loss section to see 10 or more years of annual revenue and net profit. That table is your first classification tool.

body.title: Try It on Two Stocks You Own
steps: Pick one stock you think is cyclical and one you think is defensive from your Zerodha or other demat holdings
Open each on Screener.in and go to the Profit and Loss table
Note the highest and lowest annual net profit in the last 10 years
Check whether either company reported a loss, or a profit fall of more than 30%, in any year
Compare the worst year's revenue fall with the worst year's profit fall
Decide whether your original label still holds, and write down why

cards.definition: A company whose profits rise sharply in economic expansions and fall sharply, sometimes into losses, in slowdowns.
A company whose profits stay relatively stable through booms and slowdowns because demand for its products does not depend much on the economy.
The recurring pattern of expansion, peak, slowdown, trough, and recovery in economic activity.
A fall in the valuation multiple, such as P/E, that the market is willing to pay for a stock, which can push the price down even when earnings grow.

points: Cyclical or defensive is a property of the business's earnings, not its share price
The test: what happened to profits the last time the economy slowed
Cyclicals see profits fall far more than revenue, often turning into losses at the trough
Share prices mislead because panics hit everything, defensives can derate, and cyclical stocks often turn before their earnings do
Use at least 8 to 10 years of profit history on Screener.in, covering a full cycle, before labelling any stock

body.text: CycleCo and StapleCo are illustrative companies with hypothetical figures. References to listed Indian companies are for educational purposes only and are not recommendations to buy or sell any security. Check the latest reported financials before relying on any figure.
